title: Atomics & the Memory Model
html:
std::atomic<T> makes individual reads, writes and read-modify-write operations indivisible — lock-free synchronisation for counters, flags and pointers.

Atomic counter

OperationMeaning
load() / store(v)Atomic read / write
fetch_add, fetch_sub, ++, --, +=Atomic read-modify-write; return old (fetch_) or new value
exchange(v)Set and return the old value
compare_exchange_strong/weak(expected, desired)CAS — the building block of lock-free algorithms
std::atomic_flagGuaranteed lock-free boolean (spin locks)

Publishing data with a flag

The default ordering, memory_order_seq_cst, is the easiest to reason about. release/acquire pairs are cheaper on some CPUs: everything written before the release-store is visible after the matching acquire-load. relaxed guarantees atomicity only — fine for statistics counters.

std::mutexstd::atomic
ProtectsAny block of code / several variablesOne variable
BlockingYes (threads sleep)No (lock-free for built-in sizes)
Best forInvariants spanning multiple fieldsCounters, flags, single pointers
Watch out

volatile is not for threads in C++ — it prevents some compiler optimisations for memory-mapped I/O but provides no atomicity or ordering. Use std::atomic.

Is ++x on a std::atomic<int> thread-safe? What about x = x + 1?

++x is a single atomic read-modify-write (fetch_add), so yes. x = x + 1 is an atomic load followed by a separate atomic store — another thread can update x in between, so increments can be lost.
